s12.slug: MONDAY · 3:40 AM · ESPLANADE AVENUE, THE NEUTRAL GROUND

body.text: They walked back up Esplanade from the river after three, the two miles of it, on feet that gave out somewhere around Claiborne and kept going anyway, and left Remy in the Quarter with three cousins and a balcony that wasn’t theirs. A few blocks short of Dupre Street, under the oaks, Lena sat down in the grass on the neutral ground and said she would get up again in a minute.
body.else: The band came apart at Esplanade and Broad an hour ago, the tuba first, then the snare, the trumpet still playing its two songs to itself on the way up somebody’s steps. A few blocks short of Dupre Street, under the oaks, they sat down on the neutral ground where it left them, and Lena said she would get up again in a minute.

body: There is one streetlight on this stretch, and it comes down yellow through the live oaks and lands on the wet grass in pieces. The oaks reach clear across the avenue from both sides. In the one over Jack somebody, in some year, threw beads up into the branches, and they hang there in loops, purple and green and gold, a few of them sun-bleached nearly white, one long strand stirring whenever the air does. The grass is soaked. The city is quieter now and not quiet: far off toward the river a band is still going, a trombone and a bass drum and not much else, and every so often down toward Broad somebody leans on a car horn in the rhythm of the Who Dat, a little farther away each time.

Now and then somebody goes by on the far side of the avenue, toward home: two girls in black-and-gold boas carrying their shoes; an old man in a Saints windbreaker walking a bicycle with a crawfish pot bungeed to the rack; a boy of twenty or so with HARTLEY ironed onto the back of a plain gold T-shirt, who stops under the streetlight, raises both fists at the oak, says “Who dat” up into it, conversationally, and walks on.

He has his back against the trunk and the Carhartt spread on the grass under the two of them, and the cold coming up through it. Lena is against his left side with her head on his shoulder. Her hair is down; it gave up on the pencil somewhere around midnight, and it smells of fireworks. What was left of the stranger’s fleur-de-lis has come off her cheekbone onto his shirt, at the shoulder, where her cheek is. Her knees are drawn up, and two fingers of her right hand are hooked into the placket of his shirt, at the second button. His left arm is round her, under her arm, his hand on her ribs.

Laney is asleep against Lena’s other side with her mouth open and somebody’s beads wound twice round her wrist. On the curb a few yards off Theo is awake, sitting with his good coat pulled down round his knees and his chin in the collar, turned sideways to the avenue. On the next bench Kevin sleeps sitting up, chin on his chest, the BlackBerry in one hand and his rosary in the other, and Margot sits beside him, awake, with her notebook shut on her knee and one of Kevin’s beads pinched between her finger and thumb.
“Picture it,” Theo says, to the avenue. “A city of three hundred thousand people, and not one chair.”
“You’re on a curb.”
“A curb isn’t a chair, Costigan. A curb is a *suggestion*.”
“He went under in the fourth decade,” Margot says, low, across the grass. “I’m holding his place.”
“That’s how it starts.”
“I’m a social scientist. I’m holding it *neutrally*.”
Against Lena, Laney says, quite clearly, “Not in those shoes,” and is gone again.
Lena’s fingers tighten in his shirt. Her eyes are shut. “Don’t let me sleep out here,” she says, into his shoulder. “Mama’ll kill you.”
“Me.”
“You. She likes me.”
“She sends me for ice.”
“That’s how you know,” Lena says.
Down at Broad the horn does the chant again, fainter. Lena turns her face a little further in against his shirt, so that the next thing comes out muffled, and he has to put his head down to get it.
“I wanted you here for this,” she says. “Since September.”

Her fingers come loose from the button and don’t close again. Her breathing goes long and slow and even. He looks at the part in her hair under the streetlight, and the bits of gold paint caught in it, and he opens his mouth, and whatever he had to say back to that he keeps, and after a minute she is too far under to hear it anyway.
At 3:44 the RAZR goes off against his thigh, twice.
He works it out of his jeans with his right hand and opens it against his knee, one-handed, on its cracked hinge. The little screen lights his fingers green.

body.text: i cheered for the wrong people and they lost so im taking full credit. go be loud. tell the man on the porch im sorry

body: He laughs with his mouth shut, and Lena’s head goes up and down on his shoulder with it and doesn’t wake. She sent it with the confetti still coming down in Miami, from a trailer in Burnaby, most likely, in Kyle’s cap and Cassie’s wig, and it has been six hours in the jammed air over this city looking for him. He can see her doing it: both thumbs, the cap on backward over the wig, Kyle from Fort Wayne beside her with his head in his hands. The man on the porch is asleep on Dupre Street by now, or ought to be, in his Brees jersey, with his voice gone.
He answers it. The keys go in one at a time under his thumb, slow, because it’s one hand and T9, and his other arm is still under her.

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Made me answer the question I couldn’t at the Starlite. Thursday at one in the morning, no moon at all, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook. Christmas week: Theo’s known her since they were eleven — his father’s company makes her show. She calls him Ted; nobody else does. She saw us walk into the Hallorans’ together and hid behind a ficus. “Peace mission” was for him. He ran into her at a party in the hills on the twenty-second, and she says he knows. She had me do the weather barefoot in the snow. Seventeen days; she’s not counting. Christmas morning my family found her — Gina gave me her show on DVD. They know her as the nice one. She wants it on her headstone. The day after Christmas my whole family watched season two of her show. She was eighteen, in a blazer, on a dock. She’s good — Dad said so, and she says nobody says good. Nonna prays for Cassidy now. She bought Chesterton used on Ventura without knowing it was my book, and wants to know who picked midnight. The Monday after Christmas she called, and we talked till my phone died. New Year’s Eve she watched my ball drop on the East Coast feed at nine her time and texted, so she’d be at midnight with me. Then she had her own, at three in the morning mine, from a locked den in the hills. I told her I called Ted *Ted*. She says he’s right: that one’s hers. She has my flight home written on her hand. She read Matthew 2 because I said Sunday was Epiphany; Herod is a jealous showrunner. OFFICIALLY, in eyeliner, on a sign at the rope at Santa Barbara, in sunglasses at night. A girl from my flight filmed it, and by morning it was on a gossip blog. Skye put the still on her own Facebook herself. Her people wanted lunch: her mother, Debbie, who manages her, and her publicist, Corinne. The rules: no pictures, ‘a friend from school,’ February. Take the airport down. She took it down. There was a folder with my last name on it, and she pushed it back without opening it. At a gas station in Buellton she took the first picture of the two of us herself, at arm’s length, and put it up instead. Then she changed her status herself and made me say yes to it on her phone — the first thing anybody ever watched her do that nobody wrote. Monday she came to the Fishbowl and argued with me about a rose. My pie got her out of remedial math. Tuesday she taught me stick in an empty lot — a voice for every stall. I do a bad Frank. We argued Conan. She posted a picture of me stalling. The radio, at 2:31: Haiti. At midnight she took the picture down — not for Corinne. Wednesday in the Brick she explained the plates under Haiti from her Oceanography book, read me Milton off the front of *Frankenstein*, and fell asleep on my shoulder. At the Haiti table she borrowed Becca’s apron and was Cassidy for twenty dollars a name, and asked me where God was at 4:53. Met Laney. Met everybody. Corinne wanted a statement; she told her the girl at the table was right about the pictures, and hung up. That night she asked me to say one for them, from her. ‘Saturday.’ Thursday Margot interviewed her at the Anchor; she says I’m the same in every room. Saturday at dawn she taught me again, inside the Point. Still very bad at it. She posted it and kept it up. She came to Sully’s and learned the Who Dat. Laney took a shot at her; she had it handled, she says, and I didn’t let her finish, and she says she’ll reward that sort of behavior. In the Saab I told her some about Lena — that we were close in the fall. She said she can tell there’s a rest. She drove me to confession, and went back to Sully’s without me. Saturday night she read me Sunday’s Gospel off her phone. Three nights in LA: a fitting for the wedding episode — she’s not the bride, she checked. Tuesday she made me explain Massachusetts while I walked. The tornado took Sol’s swing. Wednesday she drove home with the top down in the rain and put the two of us up on Facebook, soaked. Thursday we argued the Supreme Court under one umbrella until it turned inside out. She’s been a corporation since she was twelve — Skylark Pictures; her mother named it. She wrote my brother, in capitals; Rudy says write the number big. Friday the sun came out, and she called the telethon as Skylark. Saturday she drove six hours to the Walk for Life, walked the whole thing arguing with me, and stood in front of Clare when a man started screaming. Sunday she came to Mass. I told her why I didn’t go up. Out past the break I told her what I know about the basement, which isn’t much, and about Nonna’s question and Danny’s. She’s the answer to both. She knows there’s more; she said that’s enough. She asked me to teach her Nonna’s prayer. Monday a blog found the back of my head; Gina knew Danny’s jacket before the commenters did. Corinne called her at six: every picture of us down until there’s a strategy. At noon in her room I was the one who didn’t want to stop, and she stopped it — for Sunday. She’d read up on confession to do it: I can’t walk in on Wednesday with a plan, and she won’t be my plan. Ask her again after she’s watched me go up. She asked me what I lose when I sit in the pew, and I told her: they pass the plate over you. She watched them do it on Sunday and didn’t know what she was watching. Then she took a picture of us without looking, and that night she put it up, captioned with Corinne’s own rule — *my friend from school.* At the lunch in Studio City her shoes stayed on. When they got to Danny she came back for that and nothing else, and said his number from memory. In the car she said she’s very good at fine. She heard me tell Ma *tomorrow*, and that I think she’s the answer, and took the picture down at the Las Posas exit without a word. Sol’s swing is up. I told her I don’t care, and she could tell. She’s stopping anyway. She wants Nonna to like her. Wednesday she said Theo and Laney were running lines. Wednesday night she was at the curb when I got home from confession. She asked if I went. Then, in the middle of a bit about a Supreme Court justice, I said it first. I didn’t know I was going to. She’d been carrying it since Monday, and she was going to say it first. She said it back. Thursday she took me to a fundraiser in the Palisades and never said what for — it didn’t occur to her anybody would mind. It was for Boxer: Corinne wanted me in the picture so the march would stop being a story. She saw my face across the room and asked twice. I told her it was fine — she came to my Walk and took the other side seriously, so I could stand in hers. So she went back in and got the whole room to argue with me, the real arguments, in Gil’s living room, for two hours, and made sure every one of them knew where I stand. We stayed till the end. At a taquería at the bottom of Sunset she wouldn’t post Corinne’s picture. She blew me a raspberry and posted one of us at the table instead: we agree on each other, and we’re not just friends from school. She’s a union member. Two of them. Her father was Pat Doyle, a juicer on the Meridian lots, gone since she was four. Then she said her name. Mary Catherine Callender-Doyle. Baptized at St. Mary’s in Lancaster, named for his mother. The only name she has that her mother didn’t give her. I sent the first two to Gina for Nonna. At three in the morning I made the picture my profile picture. She says I stole her art. She says happy looks good on me. Friday she argued Margot to a draw and went home to learn lines. Saturday at the Point I told her Nonna lit a candle for Maria Caterina. Saturday night on the bluff she kept her word: tomorrow. Sunday she sat in the same pew, in a cardigan she bought for Mass, and watched me go up, and knelt. That night she asked first, before anything. I told her it’s still no, for now. And that it’s closer than it’s ever been. She asked what question she’s the answer to. I told her Nonna asked me what makes me pray. She asked if she does. Yes. She wants to be the good thing, with the lights off. I stayed. Just sleep. Monday she picked Danny’s birthday book on State Street — O’Connor, all the stories — and wrote the card herself, in capitals. She says Gretta’s the only one at that party who isn’t acting. At a red light the radio played it, the day before his birthday, and we sang it at each other with the top down. Somebody filmed it. Tuesday her people were on the phone by six. She didn’t share it; she wrote on my wall instead: bring the clean version next time. I told her I was sorry about her job. She kissed me on the Morro steps in front of everybody and told me never to apologize for making her happy. Then Danny called on his birthday and she got on the phone. She told him I tricked her. Then she told him the truth: she was about to leave when I walked over, and she still has the book, with CON crossed out. Candlemas she held my candle while I knelt. That night she came up to my room for the first time. She didn’t ask. When she asks again, she says, she wants me to have nowhere to be in the morning. She asked if there’s a version of later she’s in. Wednesday on the swing, coats on, she kept me in the daylight. She’s in Vancouver for two weeks, a pilot, from Friday. She told me to go to New Orleans and watch my Saints win. Maybe it’ll be good for you guys, she said. I said yes. Thursday we skipped the rest of the day for the Point. Sol let her into the darkroom in January, for the project. Thursday night it was full of me — asleep, the back of me on the Point, the two of us on the swing — pictures I didn’t know anybody was taking. She gave me the swing: NOT FOR POSTING. It’s in Hale’s book. She propped the door open on purpose. She asked. She was the one who said no. Her father called her Mary Kate. He left in the dark for a five o’clock call when she was four, kissed her, told her to go back to sleep, and didn’t come back. Everybody she’s ever loved had a call time. When I come back she wants the truth, to her face. I promised. She drove me up the hill at three and waited in the Saab under the bell tower with three suitcases in the back. Friday at a quarter to five she stood with us in the lot while Osei blessed the van, with her eyes shut, and looked at the water on the back of her hand. Bye, Coat check. She went north. We went south. Friday at a truck stop under Picacho Peak she called from Burnaby. Wardrobe took my flannel: Cassie wears it; it got the part. The geese are the size of Labradors. I read her one of Hale’s rude ones at the pump. Saturday night she called again after wrap, and I read her two more, on the Broussards’ front steps. I told Lena’s little sister who she is. My girlfriend. In Canada. She wants a call at the kickoff. Sunday at the kickoff I had the phone open to call her, and it rang in my hand. She was in a trailer in Burnaby in a Colts cap, wearing it into Cassie’s wig. She bought her own *Moviegoer* at the airport and read it on the plane. Being in the movie doesn’t make anything real either, she says. She owes me a picture. Not today. Her text after the game got to me at a quarter to four in the morning, on Esplanade. She’s taking full credit.

response: He shuts the phone on it and keeps it closed in his right hand on his knee, with the hinge still warm from his thumb.

choices.text: “full credit. the city says thank you. the man on the porch cried on a buick”

response: He folds the phone shut, still smiling at it, and sits with it in his fist, and the heels of his hands remember the Buick’s hood.

choices.text: “best night this city ever had. wish you could hear it”
choices.key: At a quarter to four in the morning, on Esplanade, Skye’s text found you. You told her it was the best night this city ever had, and you wished she could hear it.

response: He shuts it and holds it closed against his knee while down by the river the band, which she can’t hear, turns into something slow.

body: When he looks up from the shut phone, Theo is looking at him.

He has turned round on the curb to do it. His face is up in the streetlight, over the collar of the good coat, and it isn’t doing any of the things Theo’s face does for a living. His hands are knotted together round his knees. For as long as it takes the horn at Broad to come round once more, faint, he looks at Jack across the wet grass, and at the phone, and at the top of Lena’s head on Jack’s shoulder.
Theo shuts his eyes.
He keeps them shut. He leans his head back against the pole of a parking sign and sits there with his eyes closed and his face turned up into the light, and says nothing.

A car comes up Esplanade from the river under the oaks, slow, with the light bar on its roof dark. It’s an NOPD cruiser, with a strand of gold beads hung over the side mirror and a paper cup crushed flat under one wiper, and it pulls to the curb by the oak a car length past Theo’s shoes and sits there idling. The driver’s window comes down.

It’s Luc. He has been working the Quarter all night with every other cop in the city, and it is on him: the shirt gone soft at the collar, a long scratch across the back of one hand, his eyes red at the rims from a night of Bourbon Street. On his shoulder the radio is going, a dispatcher reading out a string of numbers in a voice as tired as his. He puts his forearm on the window frame. His eyes go over the pile on the grass: Laney with her mouth open; Kevin asleep with his rosary and Margot holding his place on it, who looks right back; Theo, whose eyes are open again. They come to his sister, asleep on the Ohio boy’s shoulder with her hand fallen open on the Ohio boy’s shirt. Then they come up to Jack’s face, and keep at it.
Jack’s left hand is on Luc’s sister’s ribs. He leaves it there. It seems like the honest thing to do.
“Get her home before the sun,” Luc says.
“Yes, sir.”

Luc looks at him a little longer, and the window goes back up. The cruiser pulls off the curb and rolls away up Esplanade toward the park, unhurried, under the oaks, until it turns, and the avenue is empty again.
“Was that a threat,” Margot says, “or a blessing.”
“Yes,” Jack says.
On the bench Margot moves Kevin’s bead along by one, and looks at it as though it did that by itself.

The phone is shut in his right hand. Lena has gone heavy all down his left side, heavier than she was an hour ago, and her hair has come across his chest, and her hand has slid off his shirt onto the Carhartt and lies there palm up. Over the Quarter, toward the river, the sky hasn’t started yet. He gives it a little under three hours. Above them in the oak the beads somebody threw up there in some other year turn on their strands when the air moves, and catch the streetlight, and turn back, and he sits under them with the cold coming up through the Carhartt and her breathing against his arm, and doesn’t wake anybody yet.

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. Veterans Day, on the bench above Campus Point: St. Martin gave the beggar half his cloak; she says everybody forgets the beggar took it. No. 9 for the reliquary. Friday the 13th, under the eucalyptus, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs: Julian asked her to dinner. So. Thursday night in the basement she played the piano properly — around the dead F. The last time she played it right in front of anybody was a November, four years ago. If you play well, she says, people ask you to play. Reading *New Moon* out of spite. Friday she signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed, with a cold. Two soups. She ate Julian’s. Mine’s on the sill for tomorrow. Ate Gloria’s soup cold out of the quart, at the sill, at six in the morning. Argued YES: a promise is made to a person, not to a reason. Wrote on my paper that I don’t believe one sentence of it. Neither does she. Mémère is lighting a candle for Nonna — the whole name. Half a name is half a candle. At the airport: Our Lady of Prompt Succor, for Nonna. She works fast. Thanksgiving: Theo said *pop* to the whole Broussard table. She asked about Theo, and Nonna, and her saint. Julian called during grace. Wes was in the kitchen. ‘Go back to your family, Youngstown.’ Handed Julian the bell rope at Sully’s. Knows I don’t work Mondays. Texted at two in the morning about Yusuf’s mother. On the lawn at four, looking at the place I wasn’t. Came to the Anchor at the end of my shift in Kevin’s car — Julian’s in Oakland, his brother’s home from the Navy. She has a paper. St. Nicholas Eve: Walgreens at half past one. I told her about Ma’s two hundred shoes; she said then we’re doing it, and we did every door in Delgado. Says I hold my phone like a hand of cards. Asked where I go. I said sometime. She said okay. Book Nine, for her Greek final: *Outis*. Nobody. In the laundry room she stepped back first. ‘Don’t make me be the one who wrecks something.’ Julian’s writing something she can’t hear yet. Twelve and oh in overtime. Her free hand found Kevin. Knows Book Nine by heart; asked me to pray at eight. Picked my best argument at the Brick: what a man says yes to. Put her phone face up next to mine and said nothing. Heard Julian’s song before anybody. ‘It’s good, Jack. It’s really good.’ Told me not to leave in the second chorus. The Advent party: I kept the whole room between us all night. She brought coffee to the white elephant, and I got it. Stole my 8-Ball. Won an argument about ‘Joy to the World’ with Isaac Watts. Didn’t play. Julian did. Friday night, half past twelve, she knocked on 412; Theo said the library. At the Mañanitas she told me about Juan Diego, who took the long way around the hill. Thirteen and oh. She texted me the number. After the Gaudete Mass she asked the 8-Ball something. Better not tell you now. Geminids from the roof without me. At Hale’s oral she’d answered him in Augustine — said my sentence was his. She defended it and won, and told him to ask where I say yes at two in the morning. Julian kissed her goodbye at his car; he’s going to New Orleans for New Year’s. Friday she knocked with two coffees and a list of every place. She played the basement piano for me, properly. Taught me a secret in the O Antiphons. Pecan at Gloria’s counter; fourteen and oh is ordained. On the Lighthouse porch she said it plain: I’d never not answered her before. Never missed Sully’s. Always came to her, whatever it was — and now I stay away. She knows something’s hurting. She didn’t make me say what. Walked past the last house to the Point for the first time all semester. The bonfires on the levee on Christmas Eve — call her from the garage. On the roof I nearly said it. The 8-Ball said ask again later. She gave me the tin to keep. I gave her Benedict. At the checkpoint she turned around and said something I couldn’t hear. Christmas week: her sister had the baby in the third quarter of the Dallas game, while they were still undefeated, so Beau didn’t get a vote. Lucille Odile — both grandmothers. Lena’s the godmother. Then they lost. The 8-Ball said very doubtful. She texts me the O Antiphons at dusk. Monday night she called at ten to one to argue about Pius, and won the point fair. I told her I’ve been sleeping in Danny’s bed. She said somebody ought to. When the Pope went down she texted within the minute: is he alright, are you. Christmas Eve she held the phone up to a bonfire on the levee so I could hear it burn. After Midnight Mass she wrote from the steps of Holy Rosary: an hour behind me, like she said. She’d mailed me *The Moviegoer* before the last night. Christmas night she told me how Réveillon went, and about the place her mother sets for her grandmother. Then she said her mama worked at Memorial. Nothing else. Holy Family: they lost to Tampa in overtime — ‘They’re resting.’ Fr. Dom took the short form; hers read the long one, and we’re not discussing it. Sunday night we whispered for two hours because Nonna was asleep in her chair, and she whispered too, from her back steps. I read her her own margins; she argued with the girl who wrote them. I told her Dad went in. ‘And Danny drank it.’ Julian calls at ten his time. Tuesday she called from behind the register at her father’s market — home field; her father’s making the musician a gumbo. I told her what Danny asked about the third. If Pop won’t get out of the truck, she says, I get in. She said she wouldn’t call as much. Then she said she’d call. Wednesday nothing. Thursday at dawn, the morning after Julian landed, she called from the river with beignets. She said she’d call. She asked if I asked Ma who the candle was for. No. You don’t. New Year’s Eve she texted at my midnight, an hour early for her. At hers it came the second the year turned — before the fireworks. I know what that means. Then the river on fire, and Julian beside it. New Year’s Day I called her from the garage at the half, and she said, You called *me*. Saturday night she called the house — Ma answered and talked to her for ten minutes. Two hours on the kitchen phone, her mother’s cordless dying twice. Her grandmother made the christening gown for Luc in 1985; it rode out the storm in Mémère’s cedar chest in Breaux Bridge. She had me be the priest so she could practice the promises. She thinks Binx doesn’t stop looking — he stops looking by himself. I told her Danny asked me something I can’t answer yet; she didn’t ask what. She asked how California was. ‘Come back, Youngstown.’ Two hours, and she never said Julian’s name. Lucille was baptized in the third quarter, and she didn’t get one word wrong. After that I called every night. Twelfth Night she got the baby in the king cake. Friday she said she hasn’t been fair to Julian, and she’s going to fix it. Sunday she landed: come find me tomorrow. Monday I couldn’t find her — not at 217, not at the twelve-ten. She came into Hale’s seminar a step behind him with a king cake, and the only chair left was next to mine. She was polite to me for fifteen minutes. Then Dido. Tuesday morning Julian put up a picture from their dinner Monday — birthday dinner, two days late. She’s tagged. She’d said call me after. I didn’t. At the mailboxes she asked about my break, and I told her as far as Denver, and Ma’s words about the coffee. ‘Tell her I’m glad.’ The baptism was lovely. Tuesday night at St. Brendan’s she had the whole thing organized by half past eight, in a whisper, and put me on the table with Becca. When the TV said trapped she left the room. Julian went. Wednesday at the table she met Skye. She said no pictures at the table, and I argued with her about it in front of everybody. That night at the desk: Skye’s envelope was the biggest. ‘Tell her thank you. From Newman.’ Thursday she took the far end of Hale’s table before anybody got there. She moved the Saints to Sully’s. Saturday in the back hall she said she changed her mind, and stood up for Laney, and said Skye gave a good performance, and wouldn’t say what she meant. At Atlanta she kept my chair till the half. At ten after three she told me the time. Wednesday at three in the morning, the aftershock, in the Fishbowl: she said I could stop whatever I’m doing. I don’t know what I’m doing. Thursday Hale read her whole name off his list. She told him Lena. Saturday she ran the van to San Francisco. Six hours, row three. She asked me if I was happy. I said yes. At the end of the Walk I asked her how she had the nerve to be mad at me. She didn’t answer. She thanked me for coming and left. Monday, when Caleb said I was on a blog, she turned a page. Hale gave her Sarah Miles to prosecute and me Sarah to defend. Wednesday at his house, with the President on, she didn’t drink her wine. A website on Monday, a bed on Tuesday, an iPad before lunch — she had the whole week. She said she had to find out about my girlfriend from a Facebook status, when we talked every single day for weeks. I told her that’s what I meant in San Francisco: she as good as told me to. She asked me if I still go up. Hale stood up and stopped it; the dog felt it through the floor. On her way out she told Hale Sarah let him believe he’d been replaced. She walked home up Del Playa with Laney. Friday in the lounge Laney found the taco picture. Lena laughed. Then she saw me. Then she read the rest of the screen and shut the laptop. Monday at the seminar she sat at the far end, and Hale kept her after with the door shut. Candlemas she carried a candle in the procession. Wednesday morning in the lobby she had a legal pad and a trip — New Orleans, Kevin’s mother’s van, her mother’s house — and she said to Theo, not to me, that her daddy says bring the Ohio boy. She was only telling him what he said. It’s not my trip. Thursday night we packed Kevin’s mother’s van without a word to each other. Everything went through Kevin and Laney. She asked Kevin for the way-back; she got it. She wrote WHO DAT · 3 DAYS on the back glass. Friday at five Skye told her to win her game. Safe flight, she said. She rode to the Rincon with her hood up. Friday in Kevin’s mother’s van, past Picacho, she said one thing to me — that I always did read a margin well — and from Tucson to New Mexico we had the worst fight we’ve ever had, in front of everybody. I said the thing about the movie called *Jack*. She didn’t say anything after that. At three in the morning, short of Van Horn, she said, Quarter tank. She bought two coffees. We talked about nothing till Balmorhea, and she fell asleep. At Fort Stockton neither of us said anything about it. Saturday in San Antonio she asked if Hale’s copy is any good. Hers is better. Sunday at the eight o’clock at Holy Rosary her mother put me in the pew between her and her grandmother. She was behind me in the line when I went up. Her grandmother put the two of us on the floor for the game, in front, where she could see us. At the onside kick she put her face in my shoulder. When it was over she came off the curb, and I caught her, in the middle of Dupre Street. At a quarter to four in the morning on Esplanade she fell asleep against me. She said she wanted me here for this. Since September.

Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished.
